title: Why We All Need to Care About Handwriting
author: Lauren Brown
summary: Lauren Brown reports a dramatic increase in students unable to write legibly or fluently, coinciding with post-COVID reliance on Chromebooks. Cognitive science shows that handwriting activates the left hemisphere regions managing planning, monitoring, and language processing—skills essential to writing and metacognition. Note-taking remains a critical mechanism for encoding knowledge and enabling retrieval practice; students who cannot write fluently lose this cognitive tool. Direct instruction requires students to respond and write during lessons, making legible handwriting foundational to learning. The shift to devices has left many students unable to compensate through typing or handwriting, creating a literacy crisis that requires explicit intervention.
points: Post-COVID, teachers report a sharp rise in students with illegible or labored handwriting, a shift that coincides with increased Chromebook use and reduced manuscript practice.
Handwriting activates the left hemisphere's planning, monitoring, organizing, and language processing regions—critical functions for writing quality and metacognitive development.
Note-taking is not a relic but a mechanism for encoding information into schema and enabling retrieval practice; students who struggle to write lose this essential cognitive tool.
In direct instruction classrooms, student writing during lessons (question-of-the-day, responding to prompts) drives encoding and retrieval; without legible handwriting, this mechanism fails.
Students who cannot write fluently or read their own notes cannot access their own knowledge during retrieval practice and assessments, compounding learning deficits.
quotes: Literacy expert and former national director of The Reading League, Laura Stewart speaks about handwriting...there's research around the areas of the brain that activate during handwriting….It's primarily in that all important left hemisphere.
I've often ruminated about what retrieval practice—that all-important tool in learning—looks like in history class. And one of the obvious answers is writing.
Note-taking isn't just a habit. It's a mechanism for encoding and retrieving knowledge.

This is not nostalgia for notebooks or handwriting for its own sake. It's about what handwriting makes possible. If students struggle to write—if it's slow or illegible—note-taking becomes a struggle.
If they struggle to retrieve, the learning won't stick.” Archived from Lauren Brown on April 21, 2026 by Tim.
